headlines.title: Renewed U.S.-Iran tension could push oil past $100: Rapidan Energy
headlines.summary: Bob McNally predicts that both Brent and West Texas Intermediate futures will jump above $100.
headlines.article_text: Rapidan Energy sees oil spike as U.S.-Iran military action risk rises Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Bob McNally, CEO of geopolitical and energy analysis firm Rapidan Energy Group said he foresees a 80% chance that the world will see "a resumption of military fighting." He predicts that both Brent and West Texas Intermediate futures will jump above $100. Iranian speaker of parliament Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has taken aim at U.S. Vice President JD Vance, calling his reaction to the Republican loss in the midterms a "losing gambler energy." A flight deck director signals an F-35C Lightning II on the flight deck aboard the USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN 71) during Exercise RIMPAC (Rim of the Pacific) 2026 while underway in the Pacific Ocean near Hawaii on July 17, 2026. Michelle Bir | Afp | Getty Images The U.S. is likely to resume military action against Iran in the coming days, a move that could send oil prices sharply higher, according to Bob McNally, CEO of geopolitical and energy analysis firm Rapidan Energy Group. Speaking to CNBC's " Squawk Box Asia ," McNally put the odds of "a resumption of military fighting" at 80% as the U.S. midterm elections recede. McNally said he expects both Brent and West Texas Intermediate crude futures to rise above $100 a barrel. The benchmarks are currently trading at about $100 and $91, respectively. watch now VIDEO 4:50 04:50 80% odds of renewed military attack in Iran, oil risk premium to head higher Squawk Box Asia Oil prices had spiked above the $100 mark ahead of the midterm elections as investors weighed uncertainty surrounding the Iran conflict and the risk of further U.S. military actions. President Donald Trump had previously said he would not launch new attacks on Iran before the elections, though The Wall Street Journal revealed that Washington had carried out limited strikes, according to U.S. officials. "President Donald Trump is determined, as a legacy item, almost at all costs, to prevent Iran from getting a nuclear weapon, having them give up their nuclear capabilities," McNally said. "The Iranian regime, on the other hand, is not willing to do it. And as long as that core difference in that deal space is absent, the escalation dynamic remains in place," he added. McNally's view is shared by other analysts, including Lombard Odier's chief economist Samy Chaar and head of investment strategy Luca Bindelli. In a Nov.4 note , they said the "lame duck" period before the new Congress is sworn in could give Trump a window to resume strikes against Iran. Any renewed campaign, however, could be constrained in duration and effectiveness by pressure on U.S. munitions supplies. Other analysts see the midterm results as creating more room for diplomacy. Norbert Rücker, head of economics and next generation research at Julius Baer said the market had become "more convinced" that the end of the midterms could provide a diplomatic off-ramp rather than lead to renewed escalation. That possibility increased with Iran reportedly sending the U.S. a nuclear proposal through Qatar, Reuters reported Friday, citing a senior Iranian official . But the proposal would be discussed only after Washington meets what Tehran described as "seven demands," ‌including an end to U.S. "acts of aggression," the naval blockade of Iranian ports and what it called economic warfare, as well as the release of Iranian assets. In return, Iran will allow ships to proceed freely through the Strait of Hormuz. The official also told Reuters that Washington was reviewing the proposal but ​declined to provide further details.
